title: A clock you can trust
teaches: Why wall clocks lie, two-phase commit and why it blocks, TrueTime's bounded uncertainty, and commit wait

blocks.text: At midnight UTC on 30 June 2012, the world's clocks counted 23:59:59, then 23:59:60, then midnight. Timekeepers add a **leap second** every few years to keep atomic time in step with the Earth's slightly slowing rotation. Linux had handled leap seconds before. This time, a bug in the kernel's timer code left part of the subsystem one second out of step with the rest. Programs waiting on short timers woke immediately, went back to wait, and woke again as fast as the processor could run.[^hrtimer] Java and MySQL processes on thousands of servers jumped to 100% CPU utilisation. Reddit went down for a time and Mozilla's servers struggled. Over the weekend, operators across the internet found that resetting the system clock to the current time cleared the CPU load.

Google was unaffected. Since 2011 it had **smeared** leap seconds. Its time servers ran their clocks slightly slow for a day leading up to the event, spreading the extra second across thousands of small adjustments so that no machine ever saw 23:59:60.[^smear] This technique works because Google's machines all synchronised their clocks with Google's time servers, so every machine was offset by the exact same amount.

Three months later, in October 2012, James Corbett and 25 colleagues at Google presented Spanner at the OSDI conference in Hollywood, California. Spanner is a database that distributes data across datacentres on several continents while still assigning every transaction a single global order, which it achieves by relying on hardware clocks. Google equipped every Spanner datacentre with GPS receivers and atomic clocks. Rather than assuming its clocks are exact, Spanner bounds their maximum drift and waits out that uncertainty.

As system designers, we should **pay only for the guarantee we need**. Spanner provides the strongest consistency guarantee a database can offer, which adds milliseconds of latency to every write and requires dedicated hardware. A designer must decide which data requires this guarantee.

parts.title: What a clock reading is worth

blocks.text: A server's clock relies on a quartz crystal that drifts by tens of parts per million, accumulating several seconds of error per day if left uncorrected. The **Network Time Protocol** (NTP) corrects this drift by querying a time server and compensating for network round-trip latency. On a good day, NTP keeps clocks within about 1 ms of each other inside a single datacentre, and within tens of milliseconds across the internet. However, a server that loses its time source, has a faulty crystal, or has its clock manually adjusted by an operator can be off by several seconds. A clock can also jump backwards, which is why the Snowflake ID generator in lesson 14 refuses to issue IDs while the system clock reads earlier than the last generated timestamp.

In lesson 13 we saw **last-writer-wins**, where replicas resolve conflicts by keeping the write with the later timestamp. When servers generate timestamps from local clocks, "later" simply means whichever clock showed a higher value. Suppose a shop's inventory count is replicated across two regions, and region B's clock is 50 ms behind region A's. A customer buys the last item in region A at 12:00:00.000, setting the count to 0. Twenty milliseconds later, a restock in region B sets the count to 10, stamped 11:59:59.970 by B's slow clock. When the replicas compare timestamps, region A's write wins because its timestamp is higher. The database discards the restock, and the shop displays zero inventory. The failure occurred simply because the system trusted two clocks to agree within 20 ms.

A timestamp can order events reliably only if every reader knows its maximum error. NTP provides a best estimate without an upper bound on error. Spanner's architecture solves two distinct problems: how to commit a transaction atomically across multiple machines, and how to assign that transaction a timestamp that orders it accurately against every other transaction globally.

A **transaction** that modifies data across two shards, such as transferring money from an account on shard A to an account on shard B, must either succeed on both shards or fail on both. The standard algorithm for this is **two-phase commit** (2PC), formalised by Jim Gray in 1978.[^gray] One machine acts as the **coordinator**, while the shards holding the data act as **participants**. In the first phase, the coordinator sends a *prepare* message to each participant. If a participant can execute its part of the transaction, it locks the relevant rows, writes the changes and its vote to its on-disk log, and replies *yes*. By voting yes, the participant promises that it will not unilaterally abort the transaction. If all participants vote yes, the coordinator writes a *commit* record to its own log, which is the exact point at which the transaction commits. In the second phase, the coordinator notifies the participants, which then apply the changes and release their locks.
The vulnerability in 2PC lies in the interval between collecting the votes and broadcasting the decision. In the simulation below, terminate the coordinator right after the participants vote.

blocks.caption: Two-phase commit between a coordinator and two shards, slowed down so that a few tens of milliseconds take 12 seconds. You can terminate the coordinator after the votes arrive, and convert each node into a Paxos group.
blocks.task: Terminate the coordinator after the votes arrive, convert each node into a Paxos group, and run the commit again

blocks.text: A participant that votes yes and receives no reply is blocked. It cannot safely commit, because another participant might have voted no, causing the coordinator to abort. It cannot safely abort, because the coordinator might have decided to commit and already notified the other shard, which then applied the transaction. Querying the other participants only helps if one of them received the coordinator's decision. Consequently, the participant must wait while holding its row locks. Every subsequent transaction that needs those rows queues behind it for as long as the coordinator remains unreachable, which may take minutes for a reboot or hours if the disk holding the coordinator's log failed. Because of this vulnerability, 2PC is a **blocking** protocol, and many distributed systems avoid cross-shard transactions entirely.

Spanner partitions data into shards and manages each shard as a **Paxos group**, typically comprising five replicas across different datacentres. One replica acts as the leader under a time-bounded lease, using the replicated log design from lesson 11. A write to a shard commits once a majority of replicas record it in their logs. In the simulation above, toggling "Each is a Paxos group" shows how Spanner prevents 2PC from blocking: the coordinator and the participants are Paxos groups rather than single machines. Both a participant's prepare record and the coordinator's commit decision are replicated via Paxos, allowing them to survive single-machine failures. If the coordinator's leader fails, another replica in its group takes over after the lease expires, reads the commit decision from its local log, and completes the protocol. Spanner still executes two-phase commit, but runs it across fault-tolerant groups rather than individual servers.

Within a transaction, Spanner uses standard two-phase locking. A transaction acquires locks as it reads or writes rows and holds them until it commits. If two transactions read the same seat as available and attempt to book it, both cannot succeed; the second transaction queues behind the first and then sees that the seat is taken. Spanner prevents deadlocks by prioritising older transactions: if an older transaction requests a lock held by a younger transaction, it forces the younger one to abort and retry, whereas a younger transaction waits if an older one holds the lock.[^wound]

This replication adds network round trips. Committing a write to a single shard requires responses from a majority of its replicas, taking about 1 ms within a single datacentre, or 30 ms to 100 ms across different coasts or continents. A cross-shard transaction requires a prepare round across each participant's Paxos group followed by a commit round across the coordinator's group. To minimise latency, Spanner lets engineers configure replica placement and designate which region holds each shard's leader, allowing them to place the leader near the clients writing the data and keep a quorum of replicas within a low-latency radius. Engineers can also place read-only replicas in distant regions to serve local reads without increasing write latency. Commit wait further extends how long a transaction holds its locks. Because a transaction retains its locks throughout the wait period, a single contended row can process at most about 1/(2ε) conflicting writes per second, or roughly 125 writes per second when ε = 4 ms. Additionally, each leader only assigns commit timestamps that fall within its active lease interval, ensuring that a newly elected leader never issues timestamps earlier than those of its predecessor.

Atomic commits across shards solve half of the problem; ordering transactions globally solves the other half. Spanner guarantees **external consistency**: if transaction T1 finishes committing before transaction T2 starts in real-world time, then T2 receives a larger commit timestamp than T1. This guarantee ensures that transaction timestamps accurately reflect the real-time sequence of events. A read at any given timestamp observes all transactions with earlier timestamps and never sees T2 without T1. External consistency is equivalent to linearizability, the strongest consistency model from lesson 13, applied to multi-shard transactions across an entire database.

Spanner's time subsystem is **TrueTime**. Each datacentre operates several time master machines; most use GPS receivers and a few use atomic clocks, ensuring that GPS antenna or satellite failures do not share failure modes with atomic clock drift. A background daemon on every server polls multiple time masters every 30 seconds. TrueTime differs from standard clock interfaces in what its API returns. Calling `TT.now()` returns a time interval `[earliest, latest]` rather than a single value, and Google guarantees that the actual physical time falls within this window. The interval's half-width, ε, represents the clock's maximum uncertainty. In the 2012 Spanner paper, ε grew from roughly 1 ms immediately after polling a time master to about 7 ms just before the next poll as worst-case local crystal drift accumulated, averaging around 4 ms.[^sawtooth]

Knowing ε, the rule for a commit is short. Choose the commit timestamp s no earlier than `TT.now().latest`, so it is not before the true time of the commit. Then wait, holding the locks and showing the result to nobody, until `TT.now().earliest` is after s, so s is certainly in the past on every clock. This is **commit wait**, and it takes about 2ε: when s is chosen, `TT.now().earliest` is 2ε below it, the width of the interval, and the clock must run that far before earliest passes s. Equally, s may be up to 2ε ahead of the true time of the commit, if the true time is at the bottom of the interval, and the wait covers exactly that. Guess how long that is with ε at 4 ms, then compare three rules.

blocks.caption: T1 commits on a server with a fast clock, and a client observes the commit and immediately starts T2 on a server with a slow clock (each clock offset by 0.9 ε). The shaded bars show the TrueTime uncertainty intervals, using illustrative times.
blocks.task: Estimate the commit wait duration, then identify the rule that preserves timestamp order when ε is 4 ms or greater

blocks.text: With local clocks, T2 can start after T1 is visible and still get the earlier stamp, which is last-writer-wins's error again. With TrueTime and no wait, the same can happen, because T1's stamp is up to 2ε ahead of the true time at which it was shown. Commit wait closes the gap: by the time anyone can see T1, every clock in the world reads past s1, so anything that starts afterwards is stamped later.

This strict timestamp ordering simplifies reads. Because timestamps reflect the exact order of commits, a read-only transaction requires no locks. It selects a timestamp, and any replica that has applied all writes up to that timestamp can serve the read directly from its multi-version storage without blocking ongoing writes. A replica far from the leader can immediately serve stale reads from a few seconds ago, or it can serve a current read after querying the leader to verify it has caught up to the latest commits. Consequently, long analytical queries and database backups can read a consistent snapshot while the database continues processing writes.

We can calculate the latency cost of a write. When ε averages 4 ms, commit wait takes about 8 ms, but Spanner executes this wait concurrently with the Paxos replication round. If the Paxos quorum requires a 30 ms network round trip, the 8 ms commit wait finishes completely within the network delay. Inside a single datacentre, where Paxos replication takes roughly 1 ms, the 8 ms commit wait dominates the commit latency. The uncertainty bound ε directly determines write performance, which is why Google installed GPS receivers and atomic clocks rather than relying on NTP's tens of milliseconds of uncertainty: an ε of 100 ms would force every write to wait 200 ms.

Spanner's first major adopter was F1, the database powering Google's AdWords advertising platform, which had previously run on a manually sharded MySQL cluster. Resharding that MySQL deployment had required years of engineering effort. The F1 team accepted higher write latencies in exchange for automatic cross-shard transactions, a relational SQL interface, and automated sharding. As the engineers documented, the latency cost was substantial: F1 commits took tens of milliseconds or more, requiring developers to structure applications around batched, parallel queries to mask the round-trip delays.

Distributed databases that run without atomic clocks apply a similar model using a wider uncertainty bound. CockroachDB, founded in 2014 by former Google engineers, uses **hybrid logical clocks**, which combine a server's physical clock reading with a monotonic counter so that a node observing a higher timestamp from another server advances its own clock to match.[^hlc] CockroachDB assumes server clocks remain within a configured maximum offset, typically several hundred milliseconds by default. Rather than pausing every write to wait out this large interval, it shifts the cost to reads: if a read encounters a value whose timestamp falls within the reader's uncertainty window, the transaction restarts at a later timestamp. This design keeps writes fast while forcing some reads to retry. Without dedicated GPS and atomic hardware, the system cannot calculate a tight real-time bound like TrueTime's; operators must configure a conservative upper bound based on expected NTP drift, which explains the large default window. Because a clock drifting beyond this configured bound would violate consistency guarantees, any node that detects excessive clock offset automatically terminates itself.

Most application data does not require external consistency. Page-view counters or user profile pictures can use the weaker consistency models from lesson 13, serving requests at local-datacentre latencies and remaining available during network partitions. Conversely, transferring funds, booking the last seat on a flight, or generating unique sequential numbers requires strictly ordered transactions that justify tens of milliseconds per write. Engineers should classify each dataset by its consistency requirements and reserve globally ordered transactions for data that cannot tolerate anomalies. In lesson 21, we will see a second benefit of accurate timestamps: a client can pass its last observed timestamp as a token to specify how current a read replica's state must be.

blocks.title: Before choosing a transaction model
points: Identify the anomalies your system must never allow, such as selling the same seat twice, creating money, or losing a write due to clock skew.
Calculate the network round trips required to commit a write based on the physical distance between replicas.
Determine your clock synchronisation error bound and define how the system handles a node whose clock drifts beyond it.
Restrict multi-shard, externally consistent transactions to the specific datasets that require them.

blocks.caption: Seven questions on clocks and commits
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: In two-phase commit, the coordinator dies after both shards have voted yes and before it sends the decision. Why may shard A not simply abort after a timeout?
choices: Aborting would release locks that other transactions are waiting on, and they would then read rows that are halfway through a change
The coordinator may already have decided to commit and logged it, so aborting could leave A undone while the decision says committed
Shard B has already applied the change on its own once both votes were yes, so A aborting would leave the two shards disagreeing
items.why: An abort rolls back a shard's tentative changes before releasing its locks, so other transactions never read partially modified rows. Rather, voting yes is a binding promise to follow the coordinator's decision. Because the coordinator may have written a commit record to its local log before failing, shard A cannot safely abort or commit until it learns that decision. Similarly, shard B does not apply its changes until it receives the coordinator's decision.

items.ask: How does Spanner stop a coordinator's death from blocking participants?
choices: Participants that time out ask each other for the decision, and commit if every one of them voted yes in the first round
The coordinator sends its decision to the client first, and the client passes it on if the coordinator dies
Coordinator and participants are each Paxos groups, so the decision outlives any machine and a new leader sends it
items.why: The coordinator writes the commit decision via Paxos to a majority of replicas in its group. If the coordinator's leader fails, another replica in the group becomes leader, reads the decision from its replicated log, and broadcasts it. Participants querying each other cannot resolve the block if none of them received the decision before the failure.

items.ask: TrueTime reports ε = 5 ms. A transaction is stamped s = TT.now().latest. What is commit wait waiting for, and about how long does it take?
choices: Until TT.now().earliest is past s, so s is in the past on every clock: about 10 ms
Until a majority of the transaction's Paxos replicas have logged it: one round trip, whatever ε is
Until the time masters' next poll narrows ε back to about 1 ms, so the stamp is precise: up to 30 s
items.why: When s is set to the latest reading, the earliest reading is 2ε below it, and the leader waits until even the earliest reading passes s. That is about 2ε, here 10 ms. The Paxos round runs at the same time but is a separate cost.

items.ask: Two regions keep copies of a stock count and resolve conflicts by last writer wins, using each region's NTP-set clock. Region B's clock is 50 ms slow. A sale in A sets the count to 0; 20 ms later a restock in B sets it to 10. What survives?
choices: The restock, because it happened later in real time and both writes carry enough precision to show it
The sale, because B's write is stamped about 30 ms before A's, so the restock is quietly lost
Neither, because the two regions detect clocks 50 ms apart and reject both writes as a conflict to resolve by hand
items.why: Because region B's clock is 50 ms behind, a write occurring 20 ms later in real time receives a timestamp 30 ms earlier than region A's write. Last-writer-wins retains the value with the higher timestamp (the sale), silently discarding the restock.

items.ask: Five replicas of a shard sit in five US regions; a majority is about 30 ms from the leader. ε averages 4 ms. Roughly what does one write cost, and why?
choices: About 38 ms, because commit wait starts only after the Paxos round and adds 2ε to it
About 8 ms, because commit wait is the only delay a Spanner write has to wait for before replying
About 30 ms, because the 8 ms commit wait runs during the Paxos round and is hidden by it
items.why: Spanner executes commit wait in parallel with Paxos replication. When reaching a majority of replicas takes a 30 ms round trip, the 8 ms commit wait finishes well before the network responses return. Inside a single datacentre, the 8 ms commit wait would account for most of the latency.

items.ask: Why can a Spanner read-only transaction run without taking any locks?
choices: It reads stored versions at one timestamp, and any replica that has applied every write up to it can answer
It reads only from the leader of each shard, which serialises reads with writes by running them in turn
It accepts that it may see half of a transaction, because read-only work such as reports can tolerate small errors
items.why: Every write keeps its version under its commit timestamp, and timestamps follow real order. A read at timestamp t sees exactly the transactions stamped before t, a consistent snapshot, without blocking writers.

items.ask: A social site stores likes on posts and also sells tickets to its events. Which design pays for the strong guarantee only where it is needed?
choices: Every write through cross-region transactions with commit wait, so that likes and tickets share one simple model
Likes in an eventually consistent store at local latency; ticket sales in a transactional database so no seat sells twice
Both eventually consistent, with a nightly job that finds tickets sold twice and refunds one buyer of each
items.why: Delayed or slightly inaccurate like counts are harmless and should be served at low latency. Selling the same event seat twice causes a real-world conflict, justifying tens of milliseconds of write latency for strongly consistent transactions.

summary: **A clock reading is an estimate.** NTP keeps servers within about 1 ms inside a datacentre and tens of milliseconds across the internet, while a faulty or reset clock can drift by seconds or jump backwards.
**Last-writer-wins with local clocks drops writes.** A clock running 50 ms slow assigns an earlier timestamp to a later write, causing replicas to discard the more recent update.
**Two-phase commit makes multi-shard transactions atomic.** Participants lock rows and vote during the prepare phase, after which the coordinator logs the commit decision and broadcasts it.

**Single-coordinator two-phase commit is a blocking protocol.** A participant that has voted yes cannot commit or abort until it receives the coordinator's decision, so a failed coordinator leaves participant locks held indefinitely.
**Spanner runs two-phase commit across Paxos groups.** Replicating the commit decision across a majority of nodes allows a newly elected leader to complete the commit if the previous leader fails.
**TrueTime returns a bounded time interval.** GPS receivers and atomic clocks keep the time uncertainty ε to a few milliseconds, averaging about 4 ms in the 2012 paper.

**Commit wait enforces a global transaction order.** A coordinator assigns a commit timestamp at `TT.now().latest` and delays releasing locks for about 2ε until `TT.now().earliest` passes that timestamp, ensuring subsequent transactions receive higher timestamps.
**Externally consistent timestamps enable lock-free reads.** A read-only query at a chosen timestamp reads a consistent snapshot from any replica that has applied writes up to that point.
**Reserve strong consistency for data that requires it.** Financial balances and seat reservations justify tens of milliseconds per write, whereas likes and page-view counts do not.

hrtimer.title: The bug
hrtimer.text: When the Linux kernel inserted the leap second, it stepped the system clock back by 1 second without updating the high-resolution timer (`hrtimer`) subsystem, leaving the timer's internal offset 1 second ahead. When a thread requested a sleep of less than 1 second, the timer subsystem calculated that the wake-up time had already passed and returned immediately. Applications using short sleep loops, including the JVM and MySQL, spun at 100% CPU. Manually resetting the system clock forced the kernel to recalculate the timer offset.

smear.title: Smearing
smear.text: Google engineers described leap-second smearing in a September 2011 blog post. Over a 20-hour window before the leap second, Google's internal NTP servers gradually slowed their clocks so that the extra second was absorbed smoothly. Several major cloud providers later adopted leap smearing, though with different window lengths and curves, meaning smeared clocks from different providers can diverge by up to 0.5 seconds during a leap-second event.

gray.title: Jim Gray
gray.text: Gray described two-phase commit in his 1978 notes on database operating systems; Butler Lampson and Howard Sturgis worked on the same problem at the same time. Gray received the Turing Award in 1998 for his work on transactions. In January 2007 he sailed alone from San Francisco to scatter his mother's ashes near the Farallon Islands and was never found, despite a search in which thousands of volunteers examined satellite images online.

wound.title: Wound-wait
wound.text: This deadlock-prevention scheme is called wound-wait. When an older transaction requests a lock held by a younger transaction, it "wounds" the younger one, forcing it to abort and retry while retaining its original timestamp. Conversely, a younger transaction waits if an older transaction holds the lock. Because younger transactions only ever wait for older ones, circular wait dependencies cannot form, and an aborted transaction preserves its early timestamp so it eventually succeeds.

sawtooth.title: Where ε comes from
sawtooth.text: Between time-master polls, a server assumes a worst-case local crystal drift of 200 microseconds per second. Over a 30-second polling interval, this drift adds 6 ms of uncertainty to the roughly 1 ms of network and reference uncertainty from querying the time masters, producing a 1 ms to 7 ms sawtooth pattern. Time masters equipped with rubidium atomic clocks (which the paper calls Armageddon masters) protect against regional GPS outages. Any server whose local clock drifts too far from the time masters removes itself from cluster membership.

hlc.title: Hybrid logical clocks
hlc.text: Sandeep Kulkarni, Murat Demirbas, and colleagues published the hybrid logical clock (HLC) algorithm in 2014. Each node maintains a timestamp combining the highest physical clock reading it has observed (either locally or in messages from peers) with a logical counter to order concurrent events. HLC timestamps preserve causal ordering like Lamport clocks while remaining close to physical wall-clock time, allowing the database to serve snapshot reads at specific timestamps.
